author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
addressee: a gathered congregation celebrating a festival of the holy martyrs
occasion: A festal assembly in honor of the holy martyrs, whose visible splendor and the fervent faith of the congregation move the preacher to speak despite his sense of inadequacy.
argument: The speaker begins by wishing to remain silent because his speech is unpolished, but the splendor of the festival and the zeal of the congregation compel him to speak. He presents the martyrs as those who strengthen the weak and draw all ages to the feast: they persuade old men to complete a long journey with much sweat, urge women to travel together with young men, and lead the infant age crawling here. The martyrs leap against death, laugh at swords, plunder the tyrant's rage, seize death as the agent of immortality, and make victory their own in their very fall, leaping through their bodies toward heaven. They scatter their own limbs in order to bind their own souls, and break the bars of life in order to open the keys of heaven. The sermon climaxes in the victory of Christ over Hades and death, quoting the taunt, 'Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, your victory?', and declares Hades and the devil plundered, stripped of ancient armor, and cast out from his own dominion.

outline.move: The preacher overcomes his reluctance to speak, praises the martyrs' power to draw all ages to the feast, proclaims their victory over death through Christ's conquest of Hades, and declares the devil stripped and cast out.

scripture: The sermon quotes Hosea 13:14 / 1 Corinthians 15:55 in a form close to the Septuagint tradition, addressing death and Hades directly: 'Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, your victory?' Modern citation: 1 Corinthians 15:55 (cf. Hosea 13:14).
uncertain: The precise date of the sermon is unknown.
